input: This abstract reports a comparison of two catalyst forms for the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde, which is a reaction of considerable interest in the context of carbon utilisation. In order to make the comparison meaningful, it is helpful to define the space-time yield, which is the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour, expressed here in kg L-1 h-1. The tests that are reported were carried out under a single set of conditions, namely a temperature of 280 °C, a pressure of 40 bar and a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, with one feed composition being used throughout. The washcoated monolith catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.93 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.27 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h on stream. The extruded pellet catalyst, by comparison, achieved a space-time yield of 0.41 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 1.03 bar and an activity loss of 16% after 100 h. It should also be noted that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, so the sensitivity of either catalyst to sulfur remains unknown. Finally, it is worth observing that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge, which makes comparisons of this kind less common than might be expected. The comparison is also unusual in that both forms were examined on the same charge basis and under the same conditions, which removes a number of the ambiguities that normally complicate comparisons drawn from separate studies reported in different parts of the literature at different times.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Two catalyst forms are compared on space-time yield, the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), at 280 °C and 40 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. The washcoated monolith gives a space-time yield of 0.93 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.27 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h. The extruded pellet gives 0.41 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.03 bar and an activity loss of 16% after 100 h. On all three measures the monolith stands ahead at these conditions: yield is higher by a factor above two, pressure drop is lower by a factor near four, and activity over the same period is better retained. The comparison is a single-condition comparison. One feed composition was tested, at one temperature and one pressure, so the ranking carries no support at other conversions or space velocities, where the pellet form's higher catalyst inventory per volume could close the yield gap. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested; the sensitivity of either form to sulfur poisoning is unmeasured, and sulfur tolerance is the property most likely to reorder the ranking in service. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which is what gives the paired figures here their weight: the monolith's yield advantage is not bought with pressure drop. The pressure-drop contrast has a plant consequence of its own. A monolith bed of the same duty imposes a smaller load on the feed compression than a pellet bed, and the difference recurs for every hour on stream, whereas the yield difference is set by the reaction conditions of the hour in question. Reactor selection between the two forms therefore turns on which of the two advantages the plant values more at its own conditions, a judgement the single-condition data inform but do not settle.
